title: Anemic vs Rich Domain Models
summary: Where business logic should actually live — scattered across service classes acting on data bags, or on the entities the logic is about — and why the anemic default is still an anti-pattern.

slides.markdown:
Two entities can hold identical fields and produce identical output, yet be built completely differently: one is a bag of getters/setters with every rule living in a service class outside it (**anemic**); the other carries its own rules as methods (**rich**). The difference doesn't show up in a single unit test — it shows up in how easy the codebase is to trust six months later.

This topic is about where business logic should live, why "it works" isn't the same as "it's well-designed," and where this debate shows up as a live design discussion in interviews.

slides.sectionTitle: The anemic domain model: data classes, logic elsewhere
slides.markdown:
An **anemic domain model** is an entity — say, `Order` — that holds only fields, getters, and setters, with zero behavior of its own. Every rule that touches an `Order` (can it be cancelled? what's its total after discounts? is it eligible for a refund?) lives instead in a separate `OrderService` class that reads and writes the entity's public fields from outside.

It's called "anemic" for exactly that reason: the object that should represent the concept has no behavior — it's drained of the logic that makes it meaningful, leaving only a container the real logic operates on from a distance.

slides.sectionTitle: Why anemic models are still an anti-pattern, even though they "work"
slides.markdown:
Anemic models pass tests and ship features, so the cost is easy to dismiss — until the rules multiply. Because nothing stops a rule from living in the *wrong* service, the same "can this order be cancelled?" check ends up reimplemented slightly differently in `OrderService`, `RefundService`, and the admin panel, each drifting a little further from the others.

Martin Fowler named this specifically as an anti-pattern for a reason beyond taste: object-oriented design's core promise — that an object encapsulates both its data *and* the rules governing that data — is broken. What's left is closer to a procedural program wearing class syntax, which forfeits the main benefit OO was supposed to provide: rules that can't be checked from the wrong place because they don't live outside the object at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: anemic model vs rich model
slides.markdown:
![Anemic: an Order with only fields, reached into by OrderService, RefundService, and AdminPanel. Rich: one Order box with its own cancel(), canCancel(), applyDiscount() methods, called via order.cancel()](assets/anemic-vs-rich.svg)

The anemic panel shows the same rule reimplemented three times from the outside; the rich panel shows the rule living once, inside the object it's about.

The visual tell for anemic: many arrows pointing *into* one data box from several service boxes. For rich: behavior methods listed directly inside the entity's own box.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: moving a business rule from a service into the entity
Compare: rich vs anemic on testability, encapsulation, discoverability
slides.markdown:
| | Anemic model | Rich model |
|---|---|---|
| Testability | Must test the service with a mocked/constructed entity for every rule | Can unit-test `order.canCancel()` directly, no service or mocks needed |
| Encapsulation | Fields are public via getters/setters — nothing stops invalid states | Invariants enforced inside the entity — `cancel()` can refuse an invalid transition |
| Discoverability | Reader must find the right service and method among many | Reader opens `Order` and sees everything it can do, in one place |
| Where it fits | Simple CRUD with genuinely no business rules | Any entity with rules, invariants, or state transitions |

**How to decide:** if a class has any rule beyond "validate and store," a rich model pays for itself quickly; pure CRUD data-transfer objects with truly no logic can stay anemic without cost.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: over-correcting into a model that violates SRP
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Rich models are better, so every rule that touches `Order` should be a method on `Order`."

**Why it's wrong:** taken too far, this produces an entity with dozens of unrelated methods — pricing math, shipping-label formatting, tax-jurisdiction lookups, email copy generation — all crammed onto one class because it happens to hold the data they operate on. That's no longer a rich domain model; it's a differently-shaped **God Object**, and it violates the single-responsibility principle by giving one class many reasons to change.

**Correct model:** put on the entity the rules that are genuinely *about its own invariants* — can it transition to this state, is this value valid for it. Logic that's really a separate concern (formatting a shipping label, calling a tax API) belongs in its own collaborator that the entity's data feeds into, not bolted onto the entity itself. "Rich" means "owns its own rules," not "owns every rule that mentions it."

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up in interviews: DDD-flavored LLD questions
slides.markdown:
Low-level design interviews for systems like a parking lot, a library, or an order-management system are implicitly testing this exact choice: where do you put the rule that a book can't be checked out if it's already on loan, or that a parking spot can't be assigned twice? Candidates who default to `LibraryService.canCheckOut(book)` reading and writing a passive `Book` are demonstrating the anemic instinct by default.

A candidate who instead gives `Book` a `checkOut()` method that enforces its own invariant, and reserves the service class for orchestration across multiple entities (finding a spot, notifying a user), signals real domain-modeling instinct — not because "rich is always right," but because they made the ownership choice deliberately instead of by default.
